title: Mezcal Hangover: Why It Hits Hard and How to Avoid It
excerpt: Does mezcal give you a hangover? Why strong, smoky mezcal can hit harder than tequila, the worm and hallucination myths, and how to sip it without a rough morning.
metaDescription: Does mezcal give you a hangover? Why strength and smoky congeners matter, mezcal vs tequila, the worm myth, and how to drink it without a rough morning.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, mezcal can give you a hangover, and for some people it gives a worse one than tequila. That isn't because mezcal is "dirty" or contains anything exotic. Properly made mezcal is 100% agave, which rules out the sugary "mixto" blends that give cheap tequila its bad name. The reasons a mezcal night can go badly are more ordinary: many bottles are stronger than standard liquor, the traditional pit-roasting adds more smoky flavor compounds than most clear spirits carry, and it's easy to keep sipping a drink that tastes complex and slow. Most of all, as with every drink, the amount of alcohol you take in matters far more than which bottle it came from.

**The quick rules:** Check the strength on the label, because a lot of mezcal is bottled well above the usual 40% and each pour packs more alcohol. Sip it in small measures the traditional way instead of taking shots. Have a glass of water alongside every copita, eat a real meal before you start, and stop a couple of hours before bed. Buy from producers who list the agave type and the certification on the bottle, and never drink unlabeled, homemade, or suspiciously cheap spirits while traveling. If you want to see where mezcal sits against everything else on the shelf, our [least-hangover alcohol ranking](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) covers the full list.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover is miserable but passes within a day. **Get medical help right away (call 911 or your local emergency number) if** someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has blue-tinged or pale, clammy skin, has a seizure, or keeps vomiting while confused. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. **Also get urgent care if** blurred vision, "snowfield" or dimmed vision, severe stomach pain, or rapid breathing appear 12 to 24 hours after drinking an unlabeled or homemade spirit, since that pattern can mean methanol poisoning. See a doctor in the next few days if hangovers are getting worse over time, you're having tremors or feeling shaky and anxious the day after drinking, or you're drinking to stop those feelings. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Does Mezcal Give You a Hangover?

It does, in the same way any alcohol does. A hangover is mostly your body dealing with the after-effects of ethanol itself: disrupted sleep, dehydration, an irritated stomach, low-grade inflammation, a drop in blood sugar, and the build-up of acetaldehyde, the toxic substance your liver makes when it starts breaking alcohol down. None of that depends on the drink being made from agave, grain, or grapes. A large amount of mezcal will produce a large hangover.

What people really want to know is whether mezcal is *better or worse* than other drinks, and here the answer has more layers. There are things working in mezcal's favor and things working against it:

**In its favor:**

- **No mixto category.** Mexico's official mezcal standard requires mezcal to be made from 100% agave. Tequila can legally be "mixto," made from as little as 51% agave sugar with the rest from other sugars, and those cheaper blends are widely blamed for the worst tequila mornings.
- **It's usually sipped, not shot.** Mezcal culture is built around slow sipping from small cups. Drinking slowly gives your liver more time to keep up and makes it easier to stop at two.

**Working against it:**

- **Higher strength.** Many mezcals, especially small-batch "artesanal" and "ancestral" bottles, are sold at 45% to 55% alcohol, compared with the standard 40% for most vodka, gin, and tequila. The same pour carries more alcohol.
- **More congeners than clear tequila.** Roasting agave in an earth pit over wood, then fermenting it in open vats with wild yeasts and distilling it in small batches, produces a richer mix of flavor compounds. Some of those are congeners, the by-products linked to worse hangovers in dark spirits.
- **Strong flavor hides the alcohol.** Smoke and sweetness make mezcal taste less "hot" than its strength suggests, so it's easy to underestimate what you've had.

So mezcal is not a magic hangover-free spirit, and it's not a uniquely brutal one either. A modest amount of good mezcal, sipped slowly with food and water, tends to be fine for most people. A night of strong mezcal shots is a different story.

## Why Mezcal Hangovers Can Feel So Bad

If you've had a rough morning after mezcal, these are the most likely reasons, roughly in order of how much they matter.

### 1. The bottle was stronger than you thought

This is the one most people miss. A standard drink in the US is about 14 grams of pure alcohol, which is a 1.5-ounce (44 ml) pour of 40% liquor. The same 1.5-ounce pour of a 50% mezcal holds about a quarter more alcohol. A 55% mezcal holds close to 40% more. Over an evening of four or five pours, that's like having an extra drink or two without noticing.

Bars that pour mezcal neat often use generous measures, and tasting flights add up fast. Check the label. The alcohol percentage is required to be printed on it, and it's the single most useful number for predicting how you'll feel the next day.

### 2. Smoky congeners

Congeners are the chemicals other than ethanol that form during fermentation, distillation, and aging. They give drinks most of their flavor, and some of them seem to make hangovers worse. In a well-known controlled study published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010, Rohsenow and colleagues gave volunteers either bourbon (high in congeners) or vodka (low in congeners) to the same breath-alcohol level. People reported worse hangovers after bourbon, even though next-day performance was impaired about equally by both. Our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains which ones matter and why.

Mezcal's production process is designed to keep flavor in. Agave hearts (called piñas) are traditionally roasted for days in a pit lined with hot stones and covered with earth, which gives mezcal its smoke. Fermentation often happens in open wooden vats with wild yeasts, and many producers distill only twice, at relatively low strength, in small copper or clay stills. Each of those steps leaves more aroma compounds in the spirit than an industrial column still would. Laboratory analyses of mezcal have found a wide range of higher alcohols, esters, and smoke-derived compounds, and the levels vary a great deal from one producer and agave species to another.

What researchers haven't done is run a head-to-head hangover trial of mezcal against tequila or vodka. So it's fair to say mezcal tends to carry more congeners than a clean blanco tequila or vodka, and that congeners are linked to worse hangovers. It isn't fair to claim a specific percentage difference in how you'll feel. For most people, congeners are the second-biggest factor, well behind the total amount of alcohol.

### 3. Methanol, briefly

All fruit- and plant-based spirits contain a small amount of methanol, because it forms from pectin in the plant material. Agave contains pectin, so tequila and mezcal both have some, as do fruit brandies and wine. Your body breaks methanol down into formaldehyde and formic acid, which is why large amounts are dangerous.

In legally produced, certified mezcal, methanol levels are capped by Mexican regulations and are far too low to poison you. Ethanol actually slows methanol processing, because your liver prioritizes ethanol. Some researchers think this delayed breakdown of trace methanol may contribute to hangover symptoms the morning after heavy drinking, but that idea isn't settled.

The real methanol risk is with **unregulated, homemade, or counterfeit spirits**, which have caused deadly poisoning outbreaks in several countries. If you're traveling and someone offers you an unlabeled bottle of "mezcal," or a price that seems far too low for the bottle, skip it. Our [Mexico travel hangover guide](/never-hungover/ultimate-mexico-travel-hangover-prevention-guide-2025) covers safe drinking on the road.

### 4. Drinking it like tequila

Mezcal isn't meant to be shot. Shots get a lot of alcohol into you quickly, before your body has registered the effect, and they push your blood alcohol up in steep spikes. That's true for any spirit, but it's an especially bad match for one that's often 45% or stronger.

### 5. The usual suspects

Everything that makes any hangover worse applies here too: drinking on an empty stomach, not drinking water, staying up late, smoking, sugary cocktails, and mixing several kinds of alcohol in one night. Mezcal margaritas and mezcal cocktails at a bar can be strong and sweet at the same time.

## Mezcal vs Tequila Hangover: Which Is Worse?

People ask this a lot, and the honest answer is that it depends on which tequila and which mezcal you're comparing. Both are agave spirits. In fact, tequila is technically a type of mezcal that comes from a specific region and is made from one species, blue Weber agave. The differences that matter for your morning are in how they're made and how they're drunk.

| | Mezcal | Tequila |
|---|---|---|
| Agave | Many species allowed; espadín is the most common | Blue Weber agave only |
| Agave content | Must be 100% agave | 100% agave or "mixto" (as little as 51% agave) |
| How agave is cooked | Often roasted in earthen pits over wood (smoky) | Usually steamed in ovens or autoclaves |
| Typical strength | Often 40% to 55% | Usually 35% to 40% |
| Congeners | Usually higher, varies widely | Lower in blanco, higher in aged reposado and añejo |
| Usual way of drinking | Sipped neat in small cups | Shots, margaritas, or sipped |

Putting that together:

- **Mezcal vs cheap mixto tequila:** a decent mezcal is often the better choice. You avoid the added sugars and unknown extras in the cheapest tequilas, and you're more likely to sip slowly.
- **Mezcal vs 100% agave blanco tequila:** the blanco tequila probably has fewer congeners and less alcohol per pour, so on paper it's the slightly gentler drink. In practice the difference will be small compared with how much you drink.
- **Mezcal vs aged tequila (reposado or añejo):** both carry more congeners than blanco. Time in oak barrels adds wood compounds, much like whiskey. The bigger difference is usually strength.

If you compare equal amounts of pure alcohol, the gap between any two well-made agave spirits is likely modest. Our full guide to [tequila hangovers](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth) explains the mixto problem in more detail.

## Is Mezcal a "Clean" Spirit?

You'll often see mezcal marketed as a pure, natural, artisanal spirit, and that's partly true. It's made from a single plant with no added sugar, flavoring, or coloring allowed in most categories, and many bottles come from small family producers. In that sense it's cleaner than a mass-market flavored liquor or a premixed cocktail.

But "clean" in the hangover sense usually means low in congeners, and that's where mezcal doesn't fit the label. The same traditional methods that make it interesting make it more complex chemically than vodka, gin, or blanco tequila. If you're very sensitive to congeners, the clearest options are still the highly filtered spirits. Our guides on [vodka hangovers](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) and [gin hangovers](/never-hungover/gin-hangover) explain why even those can leave you wrecked when the amount is high.

### Does the type of mezcal matter?

Mexico's mezcal standard sorts mezcal into three categories based on how it's made:

- **Mezcal:** can be made with more modern equipment, such as autoclaves and column stills.
- **Mezcal artesanal:** agave cooked in pits or raised ovens, often crushed by hand or with a stone wheel, distilled in copper pot stills or clay pots.
- **Mezcal ancestral:** the most traditional, cooked in pits, crushed by hand, and distilled in clay pots.

The more traditional styles tend to have more pronounced smoke and more flavor compounds. Joven (unaged) mezcal skips the barrel, while reposado and añejo mezcals spend time in wood. There's no good evidence that any one category reliably causes fewer hangovers than another, but if you've noticed that heavily smoky or barrel-aged mezcals hit you harder, a cleaner, less smoky joven is a reasonable thing to try. You can also look for bottles that state the strength clearly and choose ones nearer 40%.

## Mezcal Myths: The Worm and the "Hallucinogen" Rumor

A few stubborn myths come up whenever mezcal hangovers are discussed.

**"Mezcal makes you hallucinate."** It doesn't. This rumor comes from the similarity between the words *mezcal* and *mescaline*. Mescaline is a psychedelic compound found in peyote and some other cacti. It has nothing to do with agave and isn't in mezcal. Any strange feelings after mezcal come from the alcohol.

**"The worm is what gives you the hangover" (or "the worm cures it").** Some bottles, mostly cheaper ones aimed at tourists, contain a larva from a moth that lives on agave plants, called a gusano. It's largely a marketing tradition. Eating it won't hurt or help your hangover, and it doesn't add any meaningful chemical to the drink. Most premium mezcal producers don't use it. You may also see *sal de gusano*, a salt made with ground, toasted larvae and chili, served alongside mezcal with orange slices. It's a flavor pairing, not a remedy.

**"Agave spirits are a 'happy upper' and don't cause hangovers."** Agave spirits are often described as lighter or more energizing than other drinks. There's no good evidence that agave alcohol affects your mood or energy differently from any other ethanol. The feeling you get is shaped by how much you drink, how fast, the setting, and your own expectations.

## How to Drink Mezcal Without a Bad Hangover

None of these tips will make heavy drinking safe or guarantee a good morning. Together they make a real difference for most people.

### Before you drink

- **Eat a proper meal.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood. Protein, fat, and fiber work best. Mezcal traditionally comes with food for a reason.
- **Decide on a number.** Two or three small pours is a sensible evening for most people. Because of mezcal's strength, think of each 1.5-ounce pour of a 50% bottle as about one and a quarter drinks.
- **Start hydrated.** Have a glass or two of water in the hour before you go out.

### While you drink

- **Sip, don't shoot.** Small sips also let you taste what you paid for.
- **Use small measures.** A traditional copita or a 1-ounce pour helps keep the total down. Ask for half pours in tasting flights.
- **One water per drink.** Alcohol makes you pee more by blocking a hormone that helps you hold onto water. Matching each drink with water reduces how dehydrated you'll be.
- **Stick with one kind of drink.** There's no good evidence that mixing types of alcohol is harmful by itself, but switching between drinks tends to mean drinking more overall. Our post on the [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) breaks down the research.
- **Watch the cocktails.** A mezcal margarita or a mezcal Negroni can hold two full pours of spirit. Count the alcohol in them, not just the number of glasses.
- **Stop a couple of hours before bed.** Alcohol close to bedtime disrupts the deeper parts of your sleep, and poor sleep is a big part of why you feel awful the next day.

### Choosing a bottle

- Look for **"100% agave"** and the official mezcal certification mark on the label. Certified mezcal has to meet limits for methanol and other substances.
- Look for the **agave species** listed (espadín, tobalá, and so on) and the **alcohol strength**.
- Avoid unlabeled, homemade, or unusually cheap bottles, especially while traveling.
- If smoky mezcal seems to hit you hard, try a less smoky joven, or a 100% agave blanco tequila, and see whether you notice a difference.

For a full plan that applies to any drink, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Mezcal Hangover Cure: What Actually Helps the Morning After

There's no cure for a hangover except time. Your body has to finish clearing the alcohol and its by-products, catch up on sleep, and settle your stomach. You can make that process more comfortable, though.

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Water is fine. If you were sweating, vomiting, or had diarrhea, an oral rehydration drink with sodium and potassium can help more than water alone. Our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers when they're worth it.
- **Eat something gentle.** Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, rice, or a broth-based soup can steady your blood sugar and stomach. Something salty helps replace sodium.
- **Rest.** Sleep is one of the few things that reliably helps, because alcohol-disrupted sleep is a big part of the hangover.
- **Pain relief, carefully.** If you need something for a headache, a standard dose of ibuprofen with food is the usual choice, but it can irritate an already upset stomach. Avoid taking acetaminophen (Tylenol) on top of heavy drinking, and read our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) before you do. Ask a pharmacist if you take other medicines or have stomach, kidney, or liver problems.
- **Skip the "hair of the dog."** Another mezcal in the morning just delays the hangover and adds to the alcohol your body has to clear.
- **Coffee in moderation.** It can help with grogginess, but don't use it in place of water.

For a fuller rundown of what has evidence and what doesn't, see our [science-based hangover cure guide](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide).

### How long does a mezcal hangover last?

Most hangovers peak when your blood alcohol returns to around zero, usually the morning after, and fade within 24 hours. After a heavy night of strong mezcal, it can take most of the day. Hangovers that regularly stretch into a second day are a sign that you drank more than your body handles well. A hangover that comes with confusion, repeated vomiting, or changes in your vision is not a normal hangover and needs medical attention.

## Is Mezcal Bad for You?

Mezcal isn't more harmful than other spirits at the same amount of alcohol. It also isn't a health drink. You'll find claims online that mezcal is good for digestion, blood sugar, or bone health because agave contains fibers called fructans. Those fibers are in the agave plant, but they're broken down during cooking and don't make it through distillation in any useful amount. There is no good evidence that drinking mezcal has health benefits.

The health effects of mezcal come down to the alcohol. Heavier drinking raises the risk of liver disease, high blood pressure, several cancers, and accidents, regardless of whether the bottle is a prized ancestral mezcal or a supermarket vodka. If you drink, current US dietary guidance suggests keeping it to no more than two drinks a day for men and one for women, and less is better. Because many mezcals are stronger than 40%, a single pour can count as more than one standard drink.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people who enjoy mezcal on a night out also take a supplement aimed at hangovers. The most studied is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*). Research in animals and in the lab suggests DHM may support how the liver handles alcohol and may reduce some of alcohol's effects on the brain. Human evidence is still limited, so there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone, and it does nothing about the alcohol strength in your glass. It's a possible extra, not a replacement for pacing, food, water, and sleep.

If you want to try it, two popular, well-reviewed options are [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Mezcal can absolutely give you a hangover. The amount of alcohol you drink is the biggest factor by far.
- Mezcal has to be 100% agave, so it avoids the cheap mixto problem that gives some tequila a bad name.
- It's often stronger than other spirits and usually carries more smoky congeners than blanco tequila or vodka, both of which can make mornings worse.
- Sip it in small pours, check the strength, eat first, drink water alongside, and stop well before bed.
- Never drink unlabeled or homemade spirits, and get emergency help for signs of alcohol poisoning or vision changes after drinking.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does mezcal give you a hangover?**

Yes. Mezcal contains ethanol like any other alcoholic drink, and drinking enough of it will cause a hangover. Whether it's worse than other spirits depends on how much you drink, how strong the bottle is, and how fast you drink it. Because many mezcals are bottled at 45% to 55% and carry more smoky flavor compounds than clear spirits, a night of mezcal shots can leave a heavy hangover. A couple of slow pours with food and water usually won't.

**Is a mezcal hangover worse than a tequila hangover?**

It depends on which bottles you compare. Mezcal must be 100% agave, so it's often a better choice than cheap mixto tequila. A 100% agave blanco tequila usually has fewer congeners and less alcohol per pour than mezcal, so it may be slightly gentler. When you compare the same amount of pure alcohol, the difference between two well-made agave spirits is likely small.

**Why does mezcal give me such a bad hangover?**

The most common reasons are strength and speed. Many mezcals are much stronger than 40%, so each pour holds more alcohol, and the smoky flavor makes it easy to underestimate. Mezcal also tends to have more congeners than clear spirits because of pit roasting, wild fermentation, and small-batch distillation. Shots, sugary cocktails, an empty stomach, and late nights make it worse.

**Is mezcal a clean alcohol?**

It's clean in the sense that it's made from 100% agave with no added sugar, and it's often made by small producers. It's not clean in the hangover sense of being low in congeners. Its traditional production leaves more flavor compounds than vodka, gin, or blanco tequila. If you're sensitive to congeners, a highly filtered clear spirit may suit you better.

**Can mezcal make you hallucinate?**

No. That myth comes from confusing mezcal with mescaline, a psychedelic compound found in peyote cactus. Mezcal is made from agave and contains no mescaline. Any unusual feelings after drinking it are from the alcohol. Vision changes after drinking an unlabeled or homemade spirit are a different matter and could be methanol poisoning, which needs emergency care.

**Does the worm in mezcal cause hangovers?**

No. The larva found in some bottles is mostly a marketing tradition and doesn't meaningfully change the drink. It won't cause or cure a hangover. Most premium mezcals don't include it at all.

**What's the best mezcal hangover cure?**

There's no true cure except time. Rehydrate steadily with water or an oral rehydration drink, eat something gentle and a little salty, rest, and use a standard dose of a pain reliever with food if you need it. Avoid acetaminophen after heavy drinking, and skip the morning drink, which only delays the hangover. Get medical help for repeated vomiting, confusion, or vision changes.

**How much mezcal can I drink without a hangover?**

There's no amount that guarantees no hangover, because people respond differently. For many people, one or two small pours sipped slowly with food and water won't cause much trouble. Remember that a 1.5-ounce pour of a 50% mezcal is about one and a quarter standard drinks, so the count adds up faster than with 40% spirits.
